words.definition: A large company that operates in several different countries.
words.example: Critics argue that multinational corporations have become so powerful that they can influence the policies of national governments.

words.definition: To pay another company, often in a different country, to do work that your own company used to do.
words.example: Many Western firms outsource manufacturing to countries where labour costs are considerably lower.

words.definition: The process by which different cultures become more and more similar, losing their distinctive features.
words.example: The global spread of fast-food chains and Hollywood films has fuelled fears of cultural homogenisation.

words.definition: International trade that takes place without taxes, limits or other restrictions imposed by governments.
words.example: Advocates of free trade claim that it lowers prices for consumers and stimulates economic growth.

words.definition: A tax that a government charges on goods coming into or leaving the country.
words.example: Imposing tariffs on imported steel may protect domestic jobs but raises costs for manufacturers who rely on it.

words.definition: The policy of protecting a country's own industries by taxing or limiting foreign goods.
words.example: A return to protectionism could trigger retaliatory trade wars that ultimately harm all the countries involved.

words.definition: The unfair treatment of people, such as paying them very little, in order to profit from their work.
words.example: Consumers have become more aware of the exploitation of garment workers who produce cheap clothing for Western markets.

words.definition: The series of companies and processes involved in producing a product and delivering it to customers.
words.example: The pandemic exposed the fragility of global supply chains, leading to shortages of essential goods.

words.definition: The movement of highly skilled and educated people from one country to another where they can earn more.
words.example: The brain drain from developing nations deprives them of the doctors and engineers they urgently need.

words.definition: A country whose economy is growing quickly and becoming more industrialised.
words.example: Emerging economies such as India and Vietnam have benefited significantly from foreign investment.

words.definition: Money that people working abroad send back to their families in their home country.
words.example: Remittances from migrant workers now exceed foreign aid in many developing countries.

words.definition: A situation in which countries or groups depend on each other.
words.example: Economic interdependence between nations can act as a powerful disincentive to armed conflict.

words.definition: The idea that the whole world has become like a single community because modern communication connects everyone.
words.example: Thanks to the internet and cheap air travel, the notion of a global village is closer to reality than ever before.
collocations: the concept of the global village

words.definition: A situation that is fair because everyone has the same chances and follows the same rules.
words.example: Developing countries argue that current global trade rules do not provide a level playing field.

words.definition: To receive something good, such as a reward or benefit, as a result of your actions.
words.example: While shareholders have reaped the benefits of globalisation, many low-skilled workers in rich countries have seen their wages stagnate.

words.definition: The power of a country to govern itself and make its own laws without interference from outside.
words.example: Critics fear that international trade agreements undermine national sovereignty by limiting what elected governments can regulate.
